condition.igTitle: THE MUSCLE THAT TURNED TO CHALK
requiredObservations: a large elongated calcified soft tissue mass filling one muscle compartment of the calf with dense sheet like calcification around its rim and a more lucent centre while the tibia and fibula stay normal
The visible anatomy matches the requested AP and lateral lower leg including the calf soft tissues and the declared age and anatomical exceptions.

findings: Two views of the lower leg (tibia and fibula) are presented, consistent with anteroposterior and lateral projections

A large, well-defined, oval soft-tissue mass is present in the posterior soft tissues of the mid-calf, located between the tibia and fibula but predominantly posterior/lateral to the fibula, spanning approximately the middle third of the lower leg

The mass demonstrates a peripheral rim of dense, lobulated, popcorn-like calcification with a relatively radiolucent center containing internal calcific nodules, giving a characteristic chondroid matrix appearance
The tibia and fibula cortices appear intact without erosion, periosteal reaction, or endosteal scalloping
No fracture or bony destruction is identified
The mass appears encapsulated and does not infiltrate adjacent bone
Knee and ankle joints visible at the periphery appear unremarkable
differential: Soft-tissue chondroma (extraskeletal chondroma): most likely given well-circumscribed oval soft-tissue mass with lobulated peripheral and internal chondroid (popcorn) calcifications and absence of bony involvement
Synovial chondromatosis: possible if the mass relates to a nearby joint or bursa, given multiple calcified chondral bodies with similar matrix
Extraskeletal chondrosarcoma (low-grade): considered given large size of the calcified soft-tissue mass, though the well-defined margins and absence of bony destruction are less aggressive features
anatomyConcerns: The mass is located in the soft tissues and does not appear to arise from or invade the tibia or fibula, which would be anatomically inconsistent with a primary intraosseous lesion
No markers, side indicators, or patient labels are visible on the radiograph, limiting laterality confirmation
Ankle is only partially included on the lateral view, slightly limiting distal assessment
